title: F172 - Lesson 11: Genetic Engineering Compared to Gene Therapy
courseName: OCR Level 3 Cambridge Advanced National (AAQ) in Human Biology - Unit F172: Genetics
focus: Genetic Engineering Compared to Gene Therapy: Molecular Tools, Somatic vs Germline Boundaries, and UK Regulatory Governance
deliverable: OCR AAQ Level 3 Human Biology (Unit F172: Genetics) Lesson 11 presentation exploring recombinant DNA technology, industrial transgenics (insulin, GMOs), human somatic cell therapy, heritable germline editing risks, bioethics, and statutory UK governance (HFEA, MHRA, GTAC).

objectives.knowledge: Define and distinguish industrial/agricultural genetic engineering from human clinical gene therapy.
objectives.application: Contrast somatic cell gene therapy (non-heritable, adult tissue) with germline genetic modification (heritable gamete/embryo editing).
objectives.evaluation: Evaluate ethical dilemmas (equity, enhancement, lack of consent) and analyze statutory UK legal governance (HFEA Act 1990/2008, MHRA, GTAC).

terminology.def: Direct artificial modification of an organism's genome using recombinant DNA technology to alter traits or synthesize commercial products (e.g. human insulin in E. coli).
Targeted medical intervention introducing or altering genetic material specifically within human patient cells to treat or cure disease.
Modification of differentiated non-reproductive cells; changes are strictly non-heritable and limited to the individual patient.
Modification of human gametes or early zygotes; permanent and heritable across all future generations (strictly prohibited under UK law).
Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority: UK statutory regulator governing human embryo research and prohibiting modified embryo implantation.

slides.title: F172 Lesson 11: Genetic Engineering vs Gene Therapy
slides.subtitle: OCR AAQ Level 3 Human Biology · Unit F172: Genetics (Matt)
keyTakeaways: Clear boundary definitions between biotechnology genetic engineering and human gene therapy.
Somatic vs germline principles and UK statutory legal framework.

slides.title: Genetic Engineering: Broad Biotechnology & Transgenics
slides.subtitle: Recombinant DNA, bacterial plasmids, and industrial applications
keyTakeaways: Recombinant DNA utilizes restriction endonucleases and DNA ligase to insert target genes.
Bacterial fermentation produces recombinant human insulin, factor VIII, and somatotropin.
Transgenic agriculture (Bt maize, Golden Rice) and animal models support global industry.

slides.title: Gene Therapy: Targeted Human Clinical Medicine
slides.subtitle: Treating human monogenic pathology at its molecular genetic etiology
keyTakeaways: Targeted medical introduction or correction of genetic material in human patients.
Addresses root cause of monogenic disorders (SCID, CF, SMA, Huntington's) rather than symptoms.
Delivered via clinical vectors (AAV, Lentivirus) directly to target patient tissues.

slides.title: Comparative Matrix: Engineering vs Gene Therapy
slides.subtitle: Direct comparison across purpose, target organisms, vectors, and regulation
keyTakeaways: Purpose: Industrial/agricultural product synthesis vs curing human monogenic illness.
Organisms: Microorganisms, plants, animals vs exclusively human clinical patients.
Regulation: Environmental/food standards agencies vs human clinical regulators (MHRA, FDA).

slides.title: Somatic Cell Gene Therapy: The Clinical Standard
slides.subtitle: Non-heritable therapeutic correction in differentiated body tissues
keyTakeaways: Targets differentiated adult or pediatric somatic tissues (bone marrow, retina, neurons).
Modifications are non-heritable and perish with the treated patient's cells.
Proven NHS-approved therapies include Luxturna (RPE65 retinal dystrophy) and Zolgensma (SMA).

slides.title: Germline Gene Therapy: The Generational Frontier
slides.subtitle: Gamete and early embryo modification, heritability, and biological hazards
keyTakeaways: Modifies human spermatozoa, oocytes, or early pre-implantation IVF embryos.
Permanent genetic alterations transmitted to all descendant generations.
Catastrophic risks of permanent off-target mutations and epigenetic disruption.

slides.title: Ethical, Societal & Distributive Dilemmas
slides.subtitle: Consent impossibility, enhancement slippery slope, and healthcare equity
keyTakeaways: Future generations cannot provide informed consent to modifications made on embryonic ancestors.
Slippery slope from monogenic disease cure to non-medical enhancement ('designer babies').
Astronomical treatment pricing (£1.5m–£2.8m) creates severe domestic and global inequality.

slides.title: Regulatory Oversight: UK Statutory Governance
slides.subtitle: HFEA Act 1990/2008, MHRA clinical safety, and GTAC ethical review
keyTakeaways: HFEA enforces statutory prohibition against placing genetically modified embryos into a woman.
MHRA governs somatic clinical trial approvals, GMP manufacturing, and post-market vigilance.
GTAC provides national research ethics scrutiny on all clinical gene therapy protocols.

slides.title: Concept Mastery: Testing Core Boundaries
slides.subtitle: Diagnostic true/false scenarios addressing common student misconceptions
keyTakeaways: AAV liver infusion does NOT alter offspring DNA (somatic cells cannot enter germline).
Producing insulin in bacteria is genetic engineering, NOT human gene therapy.
CRISPR correction of human embryos intended for pregnancy is illegal under UK statutory law.

slides.title: Lesson 11 Synthesis: Key Takeaways & NEA Readiness
slides.subtitle: Distinction-level demarcation of somatic boundaries in NEA Task 2
keyTakeaways: Differentiate biotechnology engineering from human therapy in coursework introductions.
Earn Distinction marks by confirming somatic non-heritable status and evaluating MHRA compliance.
